P8k: A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. Keep in mind that it's an outsider's view of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing them. Still, it's a powerful picture. She writes that they carry their babies with them and bring them into daily adult life. Children are around people of several ages and learn by taking part, and no one exhausted parent is expected to be a child's whole social world. While a nuclear household can copy some of this, a real village can make it normal.

P21: Also, I looked in the research corpus for good documentation of a real case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people. I couldn't find one where the whole sequence is described: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. It may exist but be private, or such cases may have been referred somewhere else. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and potential victims all need access to competent help and review that isn't under the control of the home community.
